Q: Does Program Counter hold current address or the address of the next instruction? A:

The PC (Program Counter) contains the address of the next instruction-pair to be fetched from memory. There are various caveats to this statement here. The first being, that in the IAS computer both instructions (like LOAD, ADD, JUMP, SUB, etc.) and data (the actual data like the number - 50) are stored in the memory, thus making the IAS computer a stored-program concept. The stored program concept is where both the program (the several instructions that make it up) and the data are stored in the main memory, since before the IAS computer, in ENIAC (Electronic Integrator and Computer), the programmer had to manually change switches and cables to execute a program. More on ENIAC here. Thus, in IAS computer, the program can simply feed the program into memory and watch it run on its own. No need to switch cables and switches.

The important concept here is that the PC holds the address of the next instruction, not the instruction itself.

Here, as you said, the PC holds the address of the next instruction, not the instruction itself. This is because, no matter which resource you are referencing or consulting from, the generally accepted size of a PC register (in bits) is 12 bits. This is because IAS computer can hold 1024-4096 words in its main memory, where each word is made up of 40 bits. For the instruction-pair word, a word contains 2 20-bit instructions (left and right) respectively. We can further divide the first and second 20 bit instructions into its 8-bit opcode, and a 12-bit address. Refer to this image below..
Instruction Word

It is impossible for the PC to hold the whole instruction pair (word) by itself, or even just the left instruction (20-bits), thus it holds only the address of that word or instruction pair which is 12-bits in size, thus making the PC 12-bits in size in IAS computer.

I fail to understand the difference between holding the current address and the address of the next instruction. Does PC hold the two addresses in two consecutive bytes at the same time?

No, the PC does not hold two addresses in two consecutive bytes at the same time. As mentioned, it can only store one address at one time. To understand the functioning of the PC, try to imagine it like this - The PC is the switch that starts the computer. When you load a value into it, or if a value is already loaded into the PC (when you execute the value), the computer starts. The PC then loads the address (the value as mentioned above) into MAR (memory address register). MAR then requests the main memory to look up the contents at that particular address and dump the contents into the MBR (memory buffer register). It is at this moment when the contents are dumped into MBR, that at the same time, the PC is incremented by one and thus holds the address of the next instruction to be executed.

Hope this explaination cleared your doubts about PC, please feel free to correct me..

Q: Load a local file to spark using sc.textFile() A:

This error happens when you run spark in a cluster. When you submit a job to spark cluster the cluster manager(YARN or Mesos or any) will submit it to worker node. When the worker node trying to find the path of the file we need to load into spark it fails because the worker doesn't have such file. So try running spark-shell in local mode and try again,

\bin\spark-shell --master local

sc.textFile("file:///C:/Users/swaapnika/Desktop/to do list")

let me know if this helps.

Q: Using Time(0) and Datetime2(0) in SQL Server A:

Datetime2(0) means the fractional precision is 0.

I think when SQL Server stores a date in type of datetime2 then read that data, thinks that it has a datetime2 with 7 precision for millisecond then truncating it to n or 0 in this case:

For example:

DECLARE @d1 datetime2 = CAST('1968-10-23 12:45:37.1237' AS datetime2(0))
        @d2 datetime(0) =  '1968-10-23 12:45:37.1237';

SELECT @d1, @d2;

result will be

1968-10-23 12:45:37.0000000     1968-10-23 12:45:37

This (result) is same for time(0):

DECLARE @t1 time =  CAST('1968-10-23 12:45:37.1237' AS datetime2(0)),
    @t2 time(0) =  '1968-10-23 12:45:37.1237';

SELECT @t1, @t2

So, When you use datetime(0) and time(0) as type of your columns the behavior is same:

DECLARE @t table(dt2 datetime2(0), t time(0));

INSERT INTO @t VALUES ('1968-10-23 12:45:37.1237', '1968-10-23 12:45:37.1237');

SELECT * FROM @t;

result is:

dt2                 t
1968-10-23 12:45:37 12:45:37
